## Proof

We work in the quotient space $\ell_\infty / c_0$, where $c_0$ is the closed subspace of sequences converging to $0$. The quotient norm is

$$\|[x]\| = \inf_{y \in c_0} \|x + y\|_\infty.$$

Here $x = (1, 1, 1, \ldots) \in \ell_\infty$ with $\|x\|_\infty = 1$.

**Upper bound.** Taking $y = 0 \in c_0$ gives $\|x + 0\|_\infty = \|x\|_\infty = 1$, so

$$\|[x]\| \le 1.$$

**Lower bound.** Let $y = (y_1, y_2, \ldots) \in c_0$ be arbitrary. By definition of $c_0$, we have $y_n \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. Consider the sequence $x + y = (1 + y_1, 1 + y_2, \ldots)$. Since $y_n \to 0$, we have $1 + y_n \to 1$. In particular, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$, $|y_n| < \varepsilon$, hence $|1 + y_n| > 1 - \varepsilon$. Therefore

$$\|x + y\|_\infty = \sup_{n \ge 1} |1 + y_n| \ge 1 - \varepsilon.$$

Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, $\|x + y\|_\infty \ge 1$ for every $y \in c_0$. Taking the infimum over all $y \in c_0$,

$$\|[x]\| = \inf_{y \in c_0} \|x + y\|_\infty \ge 1.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining both bounds,

$$\boxed{\|[x]\| = 1}.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
